lines.text: The runway show — or catwalk show, in British English — is fashion's most theatrical moment: the point where months of design, craftsmanship, and creative vision are presented to the world in a twelve-to-twenty-minute spectacle. Preparation begins weeks before: the venue is selected and transformed — industrial warehouses, heritage buildings, parks, or purpose-built structures become stages for fashion drama. The running order is meticulously planned: each 'look' (a complete outfit) is numbered, photographed, and assigned to a specific model. Backstage, organised chaos reigns — rails of garments arranged by look number, make-up artists and hairdressers creating the beauty vision, and dressers helping models change between looks in under two minutes. The front row is reserved for fashion editors, buyers, celebrities, and influencers — the people whose coverage and orders determine a collection's commercial success. As the lights dim and music fills the space, models walk the runway at a measured pace — neutral expressions, precise turns, and a posture that showcases the garments rather than the individual. The finale traditionally sees all models walk together, followed by the designer's bow — a brief, often emotional moment of public recognition. In the digital age, shows are live-streamed globally, and social media amplifies their reach instantaneously. London Fashion Week — known for its celebration of emerging talent, diversity, and creative risk-taking — is one of the world's four major fashion weeks.
